units.text: Robert Livingston was already serving as the American ambassador in France when Monroe arrived in April 1803.

judgement.reason: The passage states Livingston was the American ambassador to France and that Monroe, after being sent in 1803, 'had just arrived from America' when Livingston met Talleyrand on April 11, 1803.

units.text: Jefferson's letter of February 3, 1803, confirms he joined Monroe with Livingston in Paris for negotiations concerning New Orleans.

citations.title: Founders Online: Thomas Jefferson to Robert R. Livingston, 3 February 1803

judgement.reason: The letter explicitly states 'we have joined mr Monroe to yourself at Paris' and discusses the object of the mission concerning Orleans, directly supporting the statement.

units.text: Madison prepared joint instructions for both Livingston and Monroe, confirming their shared diplomatic mission in France.

citations.title: Founders Online: Thomas Jefferson to Robert R. Livingston, 3 February 1803

judgement.reason: The passages state Madison drew up detailed instructions for Livingston and Monroe jointly, and Jefferson's letter confirms Monroe was joined to Livingston at Paris for the negotiation mission.

units.text: Monroe arrived in Paris on April 12, 1803, to assist Livingston with the negotiations, as documented in primary correspondence.

citations.title: Founders Online: Robert R. Livingston to Thomas Jefferson, 14 April 1803

judgement.reason: The quoted primary correspondence confirms Monroe reached Paris on 12 Apr. 1803, but the passages do not state that his purpose was to assist Livingston with the negotiations.

units.text: The mission's initial objective was to secure New Orleans, which aligns with the claim about the purpose of sending the envoys.

judgement.reason: The passages state Jefferson sent Livingston to try to buy New Orleans and Florida and Monroe to help negotiate the purchase of New Orleans, supporting the mission's initial objective to secure New Orleans.
